// budget_headroom: What a DERIVED cadence aims at, as a fraction of budget_per_day and budget_per_month. Deliberately under the caps rather than at them: the caps are guards that fail the run, and a derivation that targets a guard makes the guard the design point -- one model added and the thing meant to catch a mistake is catching arithmetic working as intended. The slack is also what a re-run or a manual trigger spends. Only fit_cadence() reads this; a cadence typed on a brand, model or trim is not held to it. At 0.9 / 0.95 the comparisons land on 6 days here (925/month, worst day 32); at 1.0 / 1.0 they would land on 5, at 976/month and 97.6% of the plan, which is the state test_headroom_is_reported_honestly already calls having no room for a re-run.

buyer.label: Chicago
buyer.// shopping: The cars being bought, by target id. This is the ONE list that says what the tool is for; nothing in the watchlist names a car as special. Everything a shopped car gets — the depth below, the newest sweep, the daily cadence, the nationwide certified watch — is derived from being named here, so changing this list changes what the API plan is spent on. It used to name the CPO watch as a target of its own; that target is derived now, so name the car and the watch follows.
buyer.// shopping_fetch: How hard a car in `shopping` is looked at. Applied over the target's own settings, so being shopped can only add depth. These four values were typed onto two BMW trims by hand until they moved here: with them on the car rather than on the decision, pointing `shopping` at any other car left it on a light one-page query on its comparison cadence while the BMWs kept full depth and a daily fetch — measured by rebuilding with shopping = ["kia-ev9"] and reading the targets back.
buyer.// comparison_fetch: Its opposite number: the layer every target NOT in `shopping` gets. `"cadence": "auto"` is the fetch schedule refusing to be a ladder. The one it replaced ran 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 / 15 days and was reverse-engineered around one make -- 13 of 29 targets took 87% of the month, the other 17 brands shared the rest, and fifteen models were fetched twice a month. That was never a judgement about those cars; it was the shape of the plan after the shopped ones had taken their share. So the share is computed instead: the shopped targets cost what shopping_fetch says, and everything else takes the fastest whole-day cadence that keeps the plan inside budget_headroom of both budgets. Shop a cheaper car and the comparisons speed up on their own -- measured: two BMW trims at 22 calls a day put the comparisons on 6 days, one Kia EV9 at 11 puts them on 3. A model or trim that types its own `cadence` keeps it and is not held to the headroom.
buyer.// cpo_watch: The nationwide certified sweep, derived once per shopped MODEL. Certified cars are the ones a manufacturer promo applies to, so this asks the whole country for the lowest-mileage certified examples of whatever is being shopped and filters to the mileage cap after — the cpo and mileage query params are unverified on this API, so the filtering happens in normalize(). Three of these were hand-written trims on the i5, i7 and iX, which meant a buyer shopping anything else got no certified watch at all. Set enabled false to switch every one of them off; a model narrows its own query or stands its own watch down with a `cpo` block beside its `trims`. Cost is len(sorts) x pages calls per fetch day, national only, so one sort over two pages every second day is 30 calls a month per shopped model.
buyer.// finance: What the car costs per month, which is the number this buyer actually decides on. A promo applies ONLY to a certified car of its own model — a non-CPO i5 finances at fallback_apr like anything else. Past its expires date a promo stops applying and the page says so; it is never silently kept alive. fallback_apr is a real rate that drifts: fallback_checked is when it was last verified, and the page warns when that goes stale.

fees.tax_note: Illinois taxes a vehicle at the BUYER's home rate wherever it is bought, so this applies to every car on the page, not just the local ones. Chicago/Cook combined — verify against the current rate before trusting a total.

// years: One EV per brand, model year 2024 and newer. The rule lives HERE and nowhere else: years resolves trim <- model <- brand <- defaults like every other parameter, and it used to be written out once per model, which is four places for one decision to rot. The range runs to 2027 because "2024 and above" has no upper bound and 2027 cars list in 2026 — every range this replaced stopped at 2026 and would have excluded them in silence.

defaults.// fuel: What powertrain a row has to have. "electric" is what this tool has always enforced, and it was enforced with no knob anywhere -- so a buyer who named a petrol car in `shopping` fetched its whole plan, kept nothing, and read "No listings found yet." under a heading naming the car. It resolves like every other filter now (defaults <- brand <- model <- trim), and "any" turns it off. The API has no fuel parameter, so this is a filter on the ROWS and never on the query: a target set to "any" still pays for every record it drops, and one left on "electric" pays for every petrol car the query hands back.

// national_only: The long tail asks the country AND the buyer's states, both. It asked only the country until the overlap log had enough days to settle it, and the answer was not the one sources_for()'s comment assumes: over 28 recorded observations the States query found 310 cars and 232 of them were invisible to National. Split by the only thing that governs it -- how big a catch the National query is allowed -- a depth=full target (~100 cars nationally) loses 21% by going national_only, and a depth=light one (20 cars, the whole country, cheapest first) loses 88%. All 28 of the LONG-TAIL TARGETS are light -- a different 28 from the 28 observations above, which is why this says which --  so their National query returns the twenty cheapest of that model IN AMERICA. The split is measured on the light targets the log could see and applied to these by depth: source_overlap() needs two sources to compare, so a national_only target cannot contribute an observation and not one of these is in the window. This used to be paid for out of freshness -- 10 -> 15 days bought the second source at the cost of seeing these models twice a month instead of three times -- and deriving the cadence paid for it out of the ladder instead. They run at the derived comparison cadence now, every sixth day on this config, five fetches a month with both queries, at 925 calls/month against 1000 and a worst day of 32 against 40. No number in this paragraph is typed anywhere any more; see buyer.comparison_fetch. The certified watches keep national_only and are not part of this -- a nationwide certified watch is national BY DEFINITION, not to save a call. How many of them there are follows buyer.shopping rather than this file, since one is derived per shopped model.
// legacy_ids: Old target ids -> new ones, so history carries over when the config is restructured. A NULL value means the opposite and is not an omission: the rows are known about and deliberately left orphaned. lucid-air-touring and -grand-touring merged into one trimless lucid-air, and 53 of the 68 rows they hold are model year 2022 or 2023 — measured, not assumed — which the 2024+ watchlist can never return again, so remapping them would publish 53 cars as current inventory that no query on this sheet could produce. chevrolet-equinox-ev-rs is the opposite case on every axis: 0 of its 31 rows are pre-2024 and its window was a SUBSET of the new target's, so its reconstructed cut-off is narrower than the truth rather than wider, which is conservative. It is mapped. bmw-i7 is one row from 2026-08-29, written when the i7 was briefly trimless, and it carries no trim at all — there is no trim target to map it to, so it stays where it is. bmw-ix-cpo is one row from 2026-08-31, from the hand-written iX certified trim that existed before the watch was derived from buyer.shopping. There is no target to map it to unless the iX is shopped, and mapping it conditionally on that would make a row appear and disappear with the buyer's mind, so it stays orphaned; naming the iX in buyer.shopping rebuilds bmw-ix-cpo under the same id and the row joins it.

i5.label: BMW i5

good: CPO promo: 2.99% APR financing on certified i5s — at today's used prices that rate changes the payment maths
Quiet, refined and built like a 5-Series; the eDrive40 is EPA-rated around 295 miles
Heavy lease-return supply keeps used prices well under new
iDrive 8.5 is quick, and most cars carry Driving Assistance packages
bad: Fast charging peaks near 205 kW and tapers early, so road trips are slower than the range suggests
Over 5,000 lb — expect tire wear and a firm ride on big wheels
Equipment varies a lot by package; two cars at the same price can be very different
watch: Confirm the software is current — early 2024 cars had bugs fixed over the air
Check which packages the specific VIN has (Driving Assistance Pro, Premium, heated seats)
The battery warranty is 8 years / 100,000 miles from the original in-service date, not from your purchase

i5.// cpo: Narrows the certified watch buyer.cpo_watch derives for this model. Optional everywhere: a model that says nothing gets a sweep of the whole model, which is what makes the watch work for a car nobody has written a line about. M60s are excluded on purpose — they are not this buyer's shopping pool, and the narrower query buys deeper coverage per call.

cpo.note: The 2.99% APR certified promo is the reason to watch these.

edrive40.note: The rear-drive i5, one half of the decision beside the i7 eDrive50.

i7.label: BMW i7

good: Depreciation is the whole story: well over $100k new, and used ones now sit far below that — the cheapest a nearly-new 7-Series has ever been
One of the quietest cars made, and the rear seat is the point — Executive Lounge cars recline the right rear seat and add the 31-inch Theatre Screen
eDrive50 is the rear-drive single-motor car, xDrive60 the dual-motor one; both are rated around 300 miles depending on wheels
Same 400-volt platform and service network as the i5, so nothing about owning it is exotic

Air suspension and big wheels: look for leaks and kerbed rims before making the drive
The battery warranty is 8 years / 100,000 miles from the original in-service date, not from your purchase

i7.// cpo: Narrows the certified watch buyer.cpo_watch derives for this model. The M70 is spelled with xDrive, so the query alone cannot keep it out — trim_exclude must. This watch has never fetched: as a hand-written trim it was stood down before its first due day on a prediction, and deriving it from buyer.shopping brings it back, which is what naming the i7 as a car being bought is supposed to mean. The prediction is worth recording because the first fetch tests it: in the i7 rows actually observed, ranks 1-42 on miles.asc are 2026 cars at 1-14 miles — new inventory, none certified — so the first certified i7 may sit below the forty-car window. The i5 version of the same recipe returns cars, and its one structural difference is a year list without the current model year. If two weeks of empty results say the prediction was right, narrow the years here rather than standing the car down.

cpo.note: The current model year is left out of THIS watch and no other, because on the i7 it is the whole window: sorting the observed i7 rows by miles and asking where the first certified car sits, it is rank 52-80 on every day the record holds and rank 6-18 once 2026 is dropped, against a forty-record window. The i5 needs no such narrowing, measured the same way on the same days: rank 3-26 with every year in.
